questions.prompt: What is the best response to the mixed outcome pattern?

choices.A: Review what produced symptom change and revise the plan to address the unresolved functional goal
choices.B: Continue the plan unchanged because symptom reduction is the most objective indicator of success
choices.C: End treatment because improvement in one outcome means the intervention has been effective overall

questions.scenarioContext: A client treated for depression has lower symptom scores after ten weeks but has begun missing more work and reports that morning routines remain unmanageable. The client values employment stability more than further symptom reduction.
questions.explanation: Lower symptom scores and worsening work functioning form a mixed result that should guide targeted revision. Declaring overall success or continuing unchanged would disregard the client's valued outcome and the functional data.

questions.prompt: Which initial plan best integrates the available information?

choices.A: Require use of the same bus so avoidance does not reinforce the student's anxiety
choices.B: Focus exclusively on relaxation because school transportation is outside counseling goals
choices.C: Pair a supported return plan with alternate transportation and coping objectives while the school addresses harassment

questions.scenarioContext: A middle school student has begun refusing school. Interviews show that anxiety rises mainly on the bus, where peers have repeatedly harassed the student. The student wants to return, and the school can provide alternate transportation while addressing the harassment.
questions.explanation: The school refusal is connected to a real environmental threat as well as anxiety, so the plan should address both. Requiring immediate use of the same bus could expose the student to continued harassment, while relaxation alone would omit the relevant context.

questions.prompt: Which step-down plan best supports sustainable continuity?

choices.A: Reduce services in stages, transfer specific tasks to chosen supports, and define indicators for renewed formal help
choices.B: End all team services at once because stable housing shows that wraparound care is no longer needed
choices.C: Keep every provider involved at the same intensity to prevent the possibility of future housing problems

questions.scenarioContext: A family has maintained stable housing for six months with help from a wraparound team. The family wants fewer formal services but still needs occasional help navigating benefits. A relative and a neighborhood organization can provide agreed support.
questions.explanation: Gradual de-intensification lets the family assume more ownership while preserving clearly defined support and reentry pathways. Abrupt withdrawal risks a gap, whereas unchanged service intensity disregards the family's gains and preference for greater independence.

questions.prompt: What should the counselor communicate?

choices.A: Research participation is required because the questionnaires are completed during intake
choices.B: Refusal may reduce access to counseling even though agency policy says eligibility is unaffected
choices.C: Counseling and research are separate choices, and the client may decline research without losing services

questions.scenarioContext: At intake, an agency invites clients to allow de-identified questionnaire data to be used in a research project. Participation is optional, declining has no effect on counseling eligibility, and the research requires a separate consent process.
questions.explanation: The agency's policy makes research optional and independent of counseling eligibility. Separate consent prevents the intake setting from creating a false impression that access to care depends on research participation.

questions.prompt: How should the counselor use the result?

choices.A: Diagnose an anxiety disorder because numerical scores are more objective than client explanations
choices.B: Clarify item comprehension, consider whether the administration was valid, and integrate other interview and observational data before interpreting the score
choices.C: Discard all formal assessment methods permanently because this administration may be invalid

questions.scenarioContext: A client obtains an extremely elevated score on an anxiety inventory but appears confused when discussing several items. The client later explains that negatively worded items were interpreted in the opposite way because of reading difficulty.
questions.explanation: Misunderstood items can invalidate the meaning of the total score, so comprehension and administration conditions require review. The result should not override contradictory information, but one flawed administration also does not justify abandoning all formal assessment.

questions.prompt: Which plan best reflects a biopsychosocial conceptualization?

choices.A: Focus only on anxious thoughts because medical evaluation found no acute disease
choices.B: Defer counseling until gastrointestinal symptoms disappear through medical treatment
choices.C: Coordinate relevant medical care while targeting avoidance, coping, nutrition routines, and gradual return to valued activities

questions.scenarioContext: An integrated care client with irritable bowel syndrome and anxiety avoids eating before leaving home, worries about urgent symptoms, and has become socially isolated. The medical team has ruled out an acute condition, and the client wants to resume shared meals and community activities.
questions.explanation: The case includes interacting physical, behavioral, emotional, and social factors, all of which can inform the plan. Treating the symptoms as exclusively psychological or delaying counseling until all gastrointestinal symptoms resolve would oversimplify the formulation.

questions.prompt: If an applicable access rule requires a readily producible electronic copy when a client requests one, which response is most appropriate?

choices.A: Provide the copy through a secure available method and charge only any permitted reasonable cost
choices.B: Require paper copies at a higher fee because paper is easier for the practice to track
choices.C: Refuse electronic access unless the client purchases the same record software used by the practice

questions.explanation: The supplied rule makes a readily producible electronic format available to the requesting client. Requiring expensive paper or proprietary software would create an unsupported access barrier.

questions.prompt: Which diagnosis is most consistent with this information?

choices.A: Somatic symptom disorder
choices.B: Factitious disorder imposed on self
choices.C: Illness anxiety disorder

questions.scenarioContext: For eight months, a client has been preoccupied with having a serious illness despite minimal physical symptoms and repeated reassuring medical evaluations. The client spends hours checking the body and researching diseases, and the anxiety causes substantial impairment.
questions.explanation: The central feature is persistent fear of serious illness despite minimal symptoms and reassuring evaluations, accompanied by excessive checking and impairment. Somatic symptom disorder instead requires distressing somatic symptoms, while no deceptive behavior is described for factitious disorder.

questions.prompt: Which planning decision is most appropriate?

choices.A: Select the cognitive-behavioral plan because counselor preference should resolve choices between suitable approaches
choices.B: Combine every technique from both approaches so that no potentially helpful intervention is omitted
choices.C: Develop the acceptable evidence-informed plan around scheduled draft submission and monitor whether it produces progress

questions.scenarioContext: A graduate student seeks counseling for perfectionism that delays completion of a thesis. Both a cognitive-behavioral plan and an acceptance-based plan could address the problem. The student prefers an acceptance-based approach and wants progress measured by submitting drafts on schedule.
questions.explanation: Both approaches are described as suitable, so the client's informed preference and measurable functional outcome can guide selection. Combining all techniques may dilute coherence, and counselor preference alone is not a sufficient reason to reject the client's choice.

questions.prompt: How should the counselor respond?

choices.A: Ask the case manager to destroy the earlier summary because revocation automatically cancels past disclosures
choices.B: Document the revocation, stop future summaries, and explain that the prior authorized disclosure cannot be undone
choices.C: Continue sending summaries until the authorization's original expiration date because it was valid when signed

questions.scenarioContext: A client revokes a written authorization that allowed monthly summaries to be sent to a disability case manager. One summary was lawfully sent before the revocation. Clinic policy makes revocation effective for future disclosures when received and documented.
questions.explanation: Under the stated policy, revocation controls future disclosures once received and documented. It does not retroactively invalidate a disclosure that was lawful when made, and the original expiration date no longer authorizes continued summaries.

questions.prompt: How should the counselor use the report in preparing for the session?

choices.A: Replace the existing counseling plan with every recommendation in the evaluation
choices.B: Set the report aside because a counselor did not administer the tests
choices.C: Review findings and recommendations relevant to Keisha's goal and note questions that require clarification

questions.scenarioContext: Keisha authorizes a neuropsychologist to send her counselor a recent evaluation before their next session. The report is 30 pages long and includes broad testing results. Keisha's counseling goal is to improve organization at work, and she has not asked the counselor to interpret the full test battery.
questions.explanation: Focused review helps the counselor prepare around Keisha's stated goal without treating a broad specialist report as an automatic counseling plan. Questions about technical findings can be identified for later clarification with Keisha or the evaluator. Ignoring the report would discard potentially useful functional information.

questions.prompt: What does attainable mean when evaluating a treatment objective?

choices.A: The objective is realistically achievable from the client's baseline with available time and supports
choices.B: The objective can be completed without discomfort, setbacks, or assistance from other people
choices.C: The objective reflects the counselor's ideal outcome even if the client doubts it can be reached

questions.explanation: An attainable objective may still be challenging, but it is feasible in light of the client's starting point, resources, and time. It does not need to be effortless, and counselor preference cannot substitute for realistic client capacity.

questions.prompt: An aptitude test is administered to applicants, and scores are later compared with their job performance after one year. This procedure primarily evaluates which property?

choices.A: Face validity
choices.B: Predictive criterion validity
choices.C: Internal consistency

questions.explanation: Predictive criterion validity examines how well an earlier score forecasts a later relevant outcome. Internal consistency concerns relationships among test items, while face validity concerns whether a measure appears appropriate on its surface.

questions.prompt: What should the records custodian do?

choices.A: Follow the normal schedule because changing it after a claim may appear suspicious
choices.B: Suspend destruction of the relevant records, preserve them securely, and document the legal hold
choices.C: Give the records to the former client so the practice no longer has a retention obligation

questions.scenarioContext: A practice receives formal notice of a malpractice claim involving a former client. The practice's legal-hold procedure requires preservation of potentially relevant records, but those records are scheduled for routine destruction next week.
questions.explanation: A legal hold supersedes routine destruction for records potentially relevant to the claim. Secure preservation and documentation protect evidence integrity; transferring the records to the client would not end the practice's obligation.

questions.prompt: What should the group leader do?

choices.A: Interrupt the scapegoating, describe the group-wide pattern, and invite each member to examine a personal contribution to the tension.
choices.B: Ask the targeted member to explain why multiple people have reached the same conclusion.
choices.C: Let the criticism continue because shared agreement indicates that the group’s feedback is accurate.

questions.scenarioContext: Several group members blame one member for “making every session tense.” The targeted member becomes quiet, while the others unite around criticism and stop examining their own contributions.
questions.explanation: The leader protects the targeted member and redirects the group from collective blame toward shared process responsibility. Majority agreement does not make scapegoating therapeutically useful or establish that one person causes the entire group dynamic.

questions.prompt: What should be explained before the client agrees to services?

choices.A: Only the intern's academic program, because supervision and alternatives are administrative details
choices.B: Nothing about training status as long as the supervisor reviews the file
choices.C: The intern's status and role, the supervisor's involvement, relevant confidentiality implications, and available service options

questions.scenarioContext: A client believes the person conducting the intake is a fully licensed counselor. The clinician is actually a graduate intern working under the direct supervision of a licensed counselor, and clients may request assignment to another available clinician.
questions.explanation: Training status, supervision, and service alternatives are material to the client's informed decision. Supervisor review does not remove the need to disclose who will provide the service and how supervision operates.

questions.prompt: Which behavioral plan is most appropriate?

choices.A: Define the charging and morning routines, reinforce on-time days with agreed weekend recreation, and track arrival time
choices.B: Remove all device access for an unspecified period after each late arrival and allow the caregiver to change the consequence
choices.C: Ask the adolescent to promise better choices and discuss lateness only when a school complaint occurs

questions.scenarioContext: A 14-year-old is frequently late to first period after staying online past the agreed bedtime. The adolescent helps create a plan, values weekend recreation with family, and can place the device in a common charging area. The caregiver can provide one consistent morning cue.
questions.explanation: The plan specifies antecedent routines, a client-valued reinforcer, and an observable outcome that can be reviewed. Unspecified punishment and occasional discussion do not create consistent contingencies or usable progress data.

questions.prompt: Which plan is most appropriate?

choices.A: Designate a qualified records custodian and create secure procedures for notice, continuity, access, and financial obligations
choices.B: Give every client the practitioner's personal passwords so clients can retrieve their own files if needed
choices.C: Leave instructions to destroy all records immediately so no successor assumes responsibility

questions.scenarioContext: A solo practitioner is developing a plan for sudden incapacity or death. The practice holds active client records, future appointments, and advance payments, but no one else currently has authority to manage them.
questions.explanation: A professional will or continuity plan should authorize a qualified person to protect records, communicate with clients, manage appointments, and address unearned funds. Sharing personal passwords or ordering immediate destruction would undermine confidentiality, access, and retention duties.

questions.prompt: What is the best response to these changes?

choices.A: Evaluate the impact with supervision, use appropriate personal support, and consider rotating duties or reducing cumulative grief exposure
choices.B: Stop all contact with grieving people outside work so emotional energy remains available for clients
choices.C: Leave bereavement counseling permanently because reduced emotional presence cannot be restored

questions.scenarioContext: A counselor has facilitated several bereavement groups in succession. The counselor now avoids calls from friends who are grieving, feels guilty when enjoying family events, and has difficulty remaining emotionally present during group members' stories.
questions.explanation: Avoidance, guilt about positive experiences, and reduced emotional presence suggest cumulative grief exposure is affecting personal and professional functioning. A layered response can address the impact while preserving client care, whereas total social avoidance or permanent departure is premature.

questions.prompt: Which fit decision is most appropriate?

choices.A: Ask the client to attend without the service dog because counseling sessions are brief
choices.B: Explain the environmental limitation and facilitate care with the available qualified counselor
choices.C: Accept the client and attempt sessions until an allergic reaction actually interrupts treatment

questions.scenarioContext: A counselor has a severe dog allergy that cannot be adequately managed in the available office. A prospective client requires a trained service dog during sessions. Another qualified counselor in an accessible suite can accept the client immediately.
questions.explanation: The counselor cannot safely provide sessions in the available space, and a qualified accessible alternative is immediately available. Asking the client to forgo a required service animal or waiting for an allergic event would place the burden and risk on the client.

questions.prompt: Which approach best supports compliant text-based communication with counseling clients?

choices.A: Use ordinary personal texting whenever a client states that convenience is the highest priority
choices.B: Use an approved secure channel, establish response and emergency expectations, and verify intended recipients
choices.C: Copy every text exchange to all treatment-team members so no message is overlooked

questions.explanation: Secure technology alone is not sufficient; clients also need clear expectations about monitoring, response time, and emergencies. Personal texting and broad copying create avoidable privacy and boundary risks.

questions.prompt: Which professional growth and advocacy response is best?

choices.A: Teach hourly workers time-management strategies before changing clinic operations
choices.B: Maintain the schedule because offering identical hours to everyone is the fairest policy
choices.C: Learn about economic access barriers and use client data to advocate for feasible scheduling or service alternatives

questions.scenarioContext: A community clinic finds that hourly workers discontinue counseling more often than salaried clients. Interviews indicate that unpaid time away from work and limited appointment hours are major barriers.
questions.explanation: The discontinuation pattern is linked to unpaid leave and limited hours, not simply individual time management. Combining contextual learning with client data supports targeted changes rather than equating identical schedules with equitable access.

questions.prompt: What should the counselor do?

choices.A: Treat the sibling as the client's clinical representative because any power of attorney covers health decisions
choices.B: Verify the document's limits and obtain treatment and disclosure decisions from the competent client
choices.C: Release updates to the sibling but ask the client to consent separately to treatment

questions.scenarioContext: A competent adult client's sibling presents a power of attorney limited to banking and property matters. The sibling demands authority to consent to counseling and receive clinical updates, but the document grants no health-care decision-making power.
questions.explanation: The document grants authority only over finances and property, not health-care consent or confidentiality. Because the client is competent, the client retains control of treatment and disclosure decisions.

questions.prompt: What should the counselor do?

choices.A: Follow the network agreement, correct any excess charges, and explain client responsibility accurately
choices.B: Collect the extra amount if clients sign a separate private-pay agreement
choices.C: Label the charge an administrative fee so it falls outside the network contract

questions.scenarioContext: A counselor is in network with a health plan whose contract prohibits collecting more than the plan-assigned copayment, deductible, and coinsurance. The counselor wants to charge clients an additional $30 per covered session to offset the contracted rate.
questions.explanation: The contract defines the amounts the counselor may collect for covered services. A side agreement or a relabeled fee cannot be used to evade the plan's balance-billing restriction.

questions.prompt: Which intervention best addresses this concern?

choices.A: Tell the client that self-criticism is irrational and should be replaced with praise.
choices.B: Avoid self-compassion because the client believes criticism supports performance.
choices.C: Practice a balanced compassionate response that acknowledges the mistake and a corrective action, then compare its effect on motivation with the harsh response.

questions.scenarioContext: A client responds to mistakes with statements such as, “I’m useless and deserve to feel bad.” The client fears that a kinder internal response would eliminate accountability and reduce effort.
questions.explanation: The intervention addresses the client’s concern empirically by combining accountability with compassion and observing motivational effects. Empty praise would not be credible, while avoiding the method leaves the belief that cruelty is necessary untested.

questions.prompt: How should the counselor respond?

choices.A: Follow the rule because standardized scores are less biased than counselor judgment
choices.B: Alter borderline scores when continued counseling appears beneficial
choices.C: Explain the instrument's limits, advocate for appropriate interpretation, and seek assessment consultation if needed

questions.scenarioContext: An agency proposes using a brief symptom screener score as the sole rule for discharging clients. A counselor is trained to administer the screener but knows that it was designed to support, not replace, broader clinical evaluation.
questions.explanation: Competence includes recognizing limits on how assessment results may be used, not only administering the tool correctly. A brief screener should inform broader evaluation rather than become an automatic discharge rule, and altering scores would invalidate the process.

questions.prompt: What is the counselor’s best intervention?

choices.A: Recommend password sharing because mutual transparency reduces suspicion.
choices.B: Explore each partner’s meanings of trust, privacy, and safety, then facilitate a mutually consented boundary rather than prescribe one.
choices.C: Recommend separate phones and accounts so the issue cannot affect the relationship.

questions.scenarioContext: One partner insists that sharing all phone passwords proves commitment. The other partner experiences the demand as controlling but worries that refusing will be seen as evidence of dishonesty. Both ask the counselor to define what trusting couples should do.
questions.explanation: The counselor helps the couple examine needs and negotiate consent without declaring a universal rule for intimacy. Prescribing password sharing could validate coercion, while technological separation alone would not resolve the underlying meanings.

questions.prompt: How should the counselor adapt the plan?

choices.A: Collaborate on realistic sleep, activity, and session objectives that fit the client's stated observance and preferences
choices.B: Treat fasting as a depressive symptom because it changes the client's usual eating and sleeping schedule
choices.C: Keep all objectives unchanged because cultural and religious practices should not affect clinical planning

questions.scenarioContext: A Muslim client explains that fasting during Ramadan, late evening family meals, and early prayer will temporarily change sleep and activity patterns. The client wants to continue counseling for depression and asks that the plan reflect these personally meaningful practices.
questions.explanation: The client has identified a temporary, meaningful context that changes what is feasible. Adapting objectives preserves treatment direction without pathologizing observance or pretending that scheduling constraints are irrelevant.

questions.prompt: What should the counselor do?

choices.A: Seek supervision promptly, reinforce professional boundaries, and arrange a careful transfer if objectivity cannot be maintained
choices.B: Tell the client about the attraction so both parties can monitor its effect on counseling
choices.C: Ignore the reaction unless the client expresses attraction or a boundary violation occurs

questions.scenarioContext: A counselor notices growing physical attraction to a client and has started dressing differently on session days and reviewing the client's messages more often than clinically necessary. No boundary violation has yet occurred.
questions.explanation: Changes in dress and unnecessary message review show that the attraction is beginning to influence professional behavior. Early supervision and firm boundaries may protect care, with transfer considered if the counselor cannot maintain objectivity; disclosing the attraction would burden the client.

questions.prompt: What should the counselor do?

choices.A: Ask which immediate concern matters most, address one step at a time, and check the client’s understanding before adding information.
choices.B: Read every form aloud so the client receives all available information during the meeting.
choices.C: Set the paperwork aside until the client appears fully calm and requests it independently.

questions.scenarioContext: At an emergency shelter after a severe storm, a client is handed several forms and pages of instructions. The client stares at the papers and says, “I can’t take in any of this.” Immediate safety and basic medical needs have already been addressed.
questions.explanation: Acute stress can reduce information processing, so prioritization, small chunks, and comprehension checks make support usable. Reading everything aloud preserves the overload, while withholding all information removes access to resources the client may need now.

questions.prompt: What is the most appropriate intake action?

choices.A: Use standard voicemail because all clients must receive identical reminder messages
choices.B: Document the client's communication preferences, explain relevant privacy limitations, and use an available safer contact method
choices.C: Stop all appointment reminders without discussing how the client prefers to receive scheduling information

questions.scenarioContext: A client shares a mobile phone with several relatives and asks the clinic not to leave voicemail or display the clinic name in text notifications. The clinic can use neutral appointment reminders or contact the client through a secure portal.
questions.explanation: Intake should establish a contact method that reflects the client's privacy circumstances and the clinic's actual capabilities. A uniform voicemail rule would create avoidable disclosure risk, while eliminating reminders without collaboration may create another access barrier.

questions.prompt: How should the counselor respond?

choices.A: Explain that the client must choose one approach so the interventions do not conflict.
choices.B: Explore how the client wants the approaches to complement each other and coordinate only with the client’s informed permission.
choices.C: Contact the healer for cultural guidance before continuing counseling with the client.

questions.scenarioContext: A Native American client says that meeting with a traditional healer is important and asks whether those practices can be used alongside counseling. The client wants to decide what, if anything, is shared between helpers.
questions.explanation: This response respects the client’s cultural resources, autonomy, and control over information sharing. Contacting the healer without permission violates the client’s stated preference, while requiring a choice between approaches imposes an unnecessary division.

questions.prompt: Which intervention should the counselor facilitate?

choices.A: Instruct the silent partner to remain in the conversation until the other feels reassured.
choices.B: Tell the pursuing partner to stop raising concerns that could overwhelm the other.
choices.C: Help the couple rehearse a time-limited pause that includes a clear statement of when they will return to the conversation.

questions.scenarioContext: During conflict, one partner becomes flooded and goes silent to calm down. The other follows from room to room, interpreting the silence as abandonment. Both want a way to interrupt this cycle without avoiding the issue.
questions.explanation: A structured pause addresses physiological flooding without turning withdrawal into indefinite avoidance or abandonment. A stated return time gives the pursuing partner predictability while both partners practice interrupting the cycle.

questions.prompt: Which professional development action is most appropriate?

choices.A: Teach clients that regular attendance is necessary before adapting any services
choices.B: Learn from qualified community and professional sources, examine the counselor's assumptions, and help the agency design feasible access options
choices.C: Refer farmworkers to counselors from the same occupational background because training cannot address the experience gap

questions.scenarioContext: A counselor begins outreach to seasonal farmworkers and initially interprets missed appointments as low commitment. A community liaison explains that unpredictable work demands, transportation, and fear of lost wages shape attendance. The counselor has little knowledge of agricultural labor conditions.
questions.explanation: The attendance pattern has credible structural explanations that the counselor initially misread as low commitment. Community-informed learning and service adaptation address both the assumption and the practical barriers without treating occupational similarity as a prerequisite for competence.

questions.prompt: What should the counselor do?

choices.A: Verify the clinic's current access information and help Jamal reconnect promptly with the medication team
choices.B: Tell Jamal that missing one appointment is unlikely to matter and wait for the clinic to contact him
choices.C: Recommend an oral substitute until Jamal locates the new clinic

questions.scenarioContext: Jamal receives a long-acting medication at a specialty clinic. He missed the latest appointment because the clinic moved, and the old telephone number now plays a disconnected message. Jamal reports no acute symptoms, and his authorization permits coordination with the clinic and prescriber.
questions.explanation: The missed appointment resulted from an outdated access pathway, so current information and prompt reconnection are the relevant supports. The medication team can determine any clinical response to the delay. Recommending a substitute would place the counselor in a prescribing role.

questions.prompt: What should the counselor do?

choices.A: Recognize the misuse of positional power, stop the sarcastic responses, and use supervision to restore respectful and consistent facilitation
choices.B: Continue emphasizing the mandate because authority is the most effective response to group resistance
choices.C: Remove the member from the group because objections show unwillingness to benefit from counseling

questions.scenarioContext: A counselor leads a court-mandated group and feels challenged by one member's frequent objections. The counselor has begun responding with sarcasm and reminding the member that attendance is not voluntary.
questions.explanation: Mandated participation increases the importance of using authority carefully rather than humiliating a member for dissent. The counselor must address the personal reaction and facilitation behavior; coercion or removal based only on objections would intensify the power problem.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes confidentiality when a client reports a completed illegal act that presents no ongoing threat and no consent, legal compulsion, or other exception applies?

choices.A: Confirm only that the person is a client because that fact is less sensitive than session content
choices.B: Maintain confidentiality and require a valid basis before disclosing any protected information
choices.C: Describe the act without the client's name because police already know whom they are investigating

questions.explanation: A completed unlawful act without an ongoing threat does not create a confidentiality exception under the stated facts. Even confirming client status can reveal protected information, so an informal police inquiry is not enough.

questions.prompt: Which response best combines staff development and advocacy?

choices.A: Train staff to explain the attendance expectations more firmly before enrollment
choices.B: Learn about the practical barriers with participants and advocate for scheduling, child-care, or delivery options that address them
choices.C: Limit future enrollment to parents who can guarantee attendance at the current time

questions.scenarioContext: An evening parenting program has high dropout among single parents. Participants report that sessions overlap with shift work and that no child care is available. Staff members have been describing the departures as lack of motivation.
questions.explanation: Participant reports identify concrete access barriers rather than lack of interest. Staff learning and feasible program changes respond to those conditions, while stricter messaging or exclusion would preserve the barrier.

questions.prompt: Which diagnosis is most consistent with this presentation?

choices.A: Anorexia nervosa
choices.B: Avoidant/restrictive food intake disorder
choices.C: Body dysmorphic disorder

questions.scenarioContext: A 13-year-old has significant weight loss and nutritional deficiency because many foods are avoided for their texture and smell. The adolescent expresses no fear of weight gain, no body-image disturbance, and no desire to become thinner. A medical condition does not fully explain the restriction.
questions.explanation: The restriction is driven by sensory characteristics and has caused weight loss and nutritional deficiency without weight-shape concerns. That pattern supports avoidant/restrictive food intake disorder rather than anorexia nervosa.

questions.prompt: What is the most appropriate plan revision?

choices.A: Develop shift-specific sleep routines and a feasible anchor period while continuing to monitor sleep outcomes
choices.B: Retain the fixed schedule because modifying an evidence-informed plan would reward nonadherence
choices.C: End insomnia work until the client obtains employment with a stable schedule

questions.scenarioContext: A client seeking help for insomnia works rotating day and night shifts that cannot be changed. The initial objective requires the same bedtime and wake time every day, and the client has been unable to follow it despite using other sleep strategies consistently.
questions.explanation: The fixed schedule conflicts with an employment condition the client cannot change, despite consistent effort with other strategies. A feasible adaptation allows the counselor to test outcomes without labeling a structural barrier as nonadherence.

questions.prompt: What should the counselor do?

choices.A: Verify the client's identity and obtain the client's valid consent before beginning telehealth services
choices.B: Accept the form because a partner may sign any document that benefits the client
choices.C: Begin treatment and ask the client to ratify the form only if a dispute later occurs

questions.scenarioContext: A telehealth consent form is returned with the client's typed name, but metadata show that it came from the partner's email account. The partner admits completing the form for the competent adult client. Practice policy requires identity verification and the client's own valid consent.
questions.explanation: A competent adult's partner cannot supply consent merely because the service may be beneficial. Identity verification and the client's own valid agreement are required before relying on the electronic form.

questions.prompt: Which maintenance plan best prepares the client for the meeting?

choices.A: Avoid all direct co-parenting meetings indefinitely so that anger cannot recur
choices.B: Depend on motivation to remain calm and contact the counselor only if another outburst occurs
choices.C: Link the early cue to a rehearsed pause, identify support after the meeting, and define when to seek follow-up

questions.scenarioContext: A client completing counseling for anger outbursts has an upcoming co-parenting meeting, a situation that previously led to escalation. The client can recognize jaw tension as an early cue and has successfully used planned pauses during recent disagreements.
questions.explanation: The plan builds on a personally recognized warning sign and a skill the client has already used successfully. Indefinite avoidance prevents practice of gains, while motivation without a specific response leaves the known trigger insufficiently addressed.

questions.prompt: How should the counselor prepare to use the measure?

choices.A: Score the blank item as zero because that produces the most conservative total
choices.B: Discard the measure and avoid mentioning it because it cannot be scored immediately
choices.C: Flag the missing item, plan to clarify it with the client, and interpret the measure only as allowed after clarification

questions.scenarioContext: Before a session, a counselor reviews a symptom measure the client completed at home. One required item is blank, and the scoring instructions do not permit the counselor to treat a missing response as zero. The incomplete measure has not yet been discussed with the client.
questions.explanation: The scoring instructions explicitly rule out substituting zero for the missing response. Preparing to clarify the item preserves the measure's intended use and avoids creating a misleading score. The incomplete form may still become usable after the client addresses the omission.

questions.prompt: What is the counselor's most professionally accountable response?

choices.A: Continue the full caseload because a valid prescription rules out professional impairment
choices.B: Limit or suspend affected duties, arrange client coverage, and resume only when competent performance is restored
choices.C: Ask clients to overlook mistakes temporarily because stopping services could inconvenience them

questions.scenarioContext: A counselor begins a prescribed medication that causes marked slowed thinking and has already led to two serious documentation errors. The counselor's physician expects the effect to continue while the dosage is adjusted.
questions.explanation: The documented cognitive effects are already impairing professional performance, regardless of the medication's lawful prescription. Protecting clients requires limiting affected work and arranging continuity until competence is restored.

questions.prompt: What should the counselor do?

choices.A: Continue using personal judgment because flexibility is the purpose of a sliding fee
choices.B: Establish transparent, relevant criteria and apply and document them consistently
choices.C: Eliminate reduced fees for all current clients without notice to avoid unequal treatment

questions.scenarioContext: A counselor grants larger fee reductions to clients the counselor personally likes and smaller reductions to similarly situated clients. The practice has no written sliding-fee criteria.
questions.explanation: A sliding-fee program can allow flexibility without basing financial access on personal preference. Written, relevant criteria and consistent documentation reduce unfair treatment while preserving reduced-fee services.

questions.prompt: Which progress-note entry is most appropriate?

choices.A: Record that Rowan completed the reflection in the agreed audio format, summarize the relevant themes and response, and state the next plan
choices.B: Document that the written homework was not completed and omit the voice memo because it used a different format
choices.C: Describe the full contents of the recording even when portions were unrelated to the counseling goal

questions.scenarioContext: Because writing is physically painful, Rowan and the counselor agreed that Rowan could complete a between-session reflection as a voice memo rather than in a journal. Rowan brings the recording to the next session and discusses two themes that emerged.
questions.explanation: The audio reflection fulfilled the adapted assignment and produced material relevant to the counseling goal. The note should document the completed task, clinical response, and next step rather than labeling a format difference as noncompletion. Unrelated recording content need not be copied into the record.

questions.prompt: How should the counselor revise the entry?

choices.A: Keep the statement as written because the client's action is sufficient to identify the intervention
choices.B: Record the counselor's breathing instruction under the intervention and the client's practice and reported change under the response
choices.C: Move the entire statement to the plan section because breathing should occur between sessions

questions.scenarioContext: A counselor's draft note states, "The client used paced breathing and reported lower tension" under the heading Intervention. It does not identify what the counselor did during the exercise. The note has not yet been signed.
questions.explanation: Separating the counselor's action from the client's response makes the note clinically interpretable. The original sentence describes only what the client did and experienced, leaving the intervention unclear. The plan section should identify future action rather than replace documentation of what occurred.

questions.prompt: Which element is most characteristic of an aftercare plan?

choices.A: A detailed reconstruction of every topic discussed during active treatment
choices.B: Specific post-treatment supports, responsibilities, and contingencies for maintaining gains
choices.C: A statement that the client may contact any provider if a future problem develops

questions.explanation: Aftercare is future-focused and identifies how gains will be supported after active treatment ends. A historical reconstruction or a vague invitation to contact any provider does not assign concrete actions or contingencies.

questions.prompt: Which case-conference agenda is most likely to produce effective stakeholder coordination?

choices.A: A complete retelling of the client's history followed by open discussion with no assigned follow-up
choices.B: Separate presentations ranked by each participant's professional seniority
choices.C: Client-defined goals, decisions needed, participant responsibilities, and a method and date for follow-up

questions.explanation: This agenda links the meeting to the client's aims and converts discussion into accountable next steps. Decisions, responsibilities, and follow-up make coordination observable after the meeting. Professional seniority is not a substitute for a task-focused plan.

questions.prompt: When is a structured round especially useful in group counseling?

choices.A: When the leader wants every member to agree with a single interpretation.
choices.B: When a focused prompt can help balance participation and briefly hear from each willing member.
choices.C: When one member needs uninterrupted time for an extended individual counseling exchange.

questions.explanation: A round provides structure and broad access to participation around a defined question while allowing members to pass. It is not designed to manufacture agreement or create an extended individual session within the group.

questions.prompt: What should the counselor do?

choices.A: Respond within the disclosed service window and reinforce the messaging expectations if needed
choices.B: Treat the message as an emergency because every after-hours client contact requires immediate action
choices.C: Close the portal account because the client sent a message outside business hours

questions.scenarioContext: A secure messaging agreement states that the counselor reviews portal messages on business days, responds within two business days, and does not provide emergency coverage through the portal. A client sends a nonurgent scheduling question late Friday evening.
questions.explanation: The message is nonurgent and falls within the portal terms that the client received. An after-hours timestamp does not transform it into an emergency or justify removing access; the counselor should follow the stated response window.

questions.prompt: Which continuity response is most appropriate?

choices.A: Treat the parent's panic within the child's sessions because caregiver functioning affects the child
choices.B: Tell the parent to find care independently so the child's counseling remains completely separate
choices.C: Provide an appropriate adult referral and, with permission, coordinate only the caregiver support relevant to the child's plan

questions.scenarioContext: The parent of a child receiving counseling reports untreated panic symptoms and asks the child's counselor to provide therapy for the parent during the child's sessions. The parent is willing to seek a separate provider, and the child's progress depends partly on the parent's ability to follow the home plan.
questions.explanation: The parent's needs warrant their own provider rather than being treated within the child's sessions. Limited, authorized coordination can still support implementation of the child's home plan without making the parent a second client in that treatment.

questions.prompt: What is the primary purpose of an exception question in solution-focused counseling?

choices.A: To determine whether the client is minimizing how often the problem occurs.
choices.B: To identify times the problem is absent or less intense and examine resources associated with those times.
choices.C: To uncover the early experience that originally caused the current problem.

questions.explanation: Exception questions help clients notice existing strengths, contextual differences, and behaviors linked to better moments. They are not primarily tools for testing honesty or tracing a problem to its origin.

questions.prompt: Which in-session intervention would be most useful?

choices.A: Ask the client to suppress angry thoughts as soon as an argument begins.
choices.B: Focus exclusively on the consequences of past outbursts to increase motivation.
choices.C: Map a recent episode step by step to identify triggers, early body cues, actions, and points for a different response.

questions.scenarioContext: A client wants to stop escalating minor disagreements into angry outbursts. The client usually notices the problem only after shouting and says, “It happens too fast to change.”
questions.explanation: A detailed behavior chain slows the sequence and identifies earlier intervention points that the client currently misses. Thought suppression is unlikely to teach regulation, and consequences alone do not reveal where a different response can be inserted.

questions.prompt: A client converses comfortably in English but requests a qualified interpreter for complex counseling discussions. What is the best response?

choices.A: Decline because conversational English shows that interpretation is unnecessary
choices.B: Ask a bilingual relative to remain available only if the client becomes confused
choices.C: Arrange qualified interpretation in the client's preferred language rather than assuming conversational fluency is sufficient

questions.explanation: Everyday conversation does not establish that a client can fully understand or express complex counseling content in English. The client's request is direct information about what support is needed for meaningful participation. A relative is not an equivalent substitute for qualified interpretation.

questions.prompt: How should a counselor evaluate this opportunity?

choices.A: Compare the course with credible competency standards, evidence, instructor qualifications, and opportunities to demonstrate skill
choices.B: Enroll because use of the word certified means the title is recognized across counseling settings
choices.C: Enroll if the counselor already treats trauma because experience will supply all missing training components

questions.scenarioContext: An advertisement promises a "certified trauma expert" title after a six-hour self-paced course. It gives no information about instructor qualifications, skill assessment, supervised practice, or recognition by a professional body.
questions.explanation: A certificate label does not establish that training meets meaningful professional standards. Evaluating instruction, evidence, assessed practice, and recognition helps the counselor distinguish a marketing title from genuine competence development.

questions.prompt: What should the counselor do?

choices.A: Promptly use supervision and recovery supports to assess functioning and arrange transfer if competent care cannot be maintained
choices.B: Disclose the counselor's recovery history so the client can avoid descriptions that trigger cravings
choices.C: Continue without consultation because personal recovery should make the counselor more effective with substance-use concerns

questions.scenarioContext: A counselor in stable recovery from stimulant use begins treating a client who describes recent use in vivid detail. After several sessions, the counselor notices unexpected cravings and increasing difficulty concentrating during the client's appointments.
questions.explanation: The emerging cravings and concentration difficulty require prompt evaluation of both counselor wellness and client care. Supervision and recovery supports may permit safe continuation, but transfer is appropriate if functioning cannot be stabilized; client disclosure would shift responsibility inappropriately.

questions.prompt: How should the counselor address this issue in the plan?

choices.A: Begin the standard exercises because temporary physical sensations are the intended part of treatment
choices.B: Coordinate appropriate medical input and use suitable plan components while clarifying which exercises are safe
choices.C: Remove all exposure-based goals permanently because any seizure history rules out behavioral treatment

questions.scenarioContext: A client with panic disorder and a seizure disorder is considering interoceptive exposure exercises that deliberately produce dizziness and rapid breathing. The counselor has no information about whether those exercises are medically appropriate for this client.
questions.explanation: Deliberately provoking physical sensations warrants clarification because the client's seizure disorder may affect exercise selection. The counselor need not assume either that every standard exercise is safe or that all behavioral treatment is permanently contraindicated.

questions.prompt: What is the most appropriate response?

choices.A: Provide the information because shared-community disclosure is necessary for cultural trust.
choices.B: Decline the questions without discussion because any personal inquiry threatens professional boundaries.
choices.C: Explore what the information would mean to the client, explain the privacy limit, and discuss safer ways to address the need for understanding.

questions.scenarioContext: A client who lives in the same small community as the counselor asks for the counselor’s street and the school attended by the counselor’s children. The client says, “It would help me know you understand people like us.”
questions.explanation: The counselor maintains personal and family privacy while treating the request as meaningful rather than simply rejecting it. Exploring the underlying need can lead to appropriate ways of building cultural trust without disclosing identifying details.

questions.prompt: Which response is most likely to support de-escalation?

choices.A: Explain all reasons the request was denied so the client understands the agency’s decision.
choices.B: Tell the client that the meeting will end unless the interruptions stop immediately.
choices.C: Lower the pace, reflect the urgent need behind the anger, and offer a choice between reviewing an appeal step or identifying another resource.

questions.scenarioContext: A client at a community agency begins shouting after learning that an assistance request was denied. The client is not threatening anyone but repeatedly interrupts and demands that the counselor “fix it now.”
questions.explanation: This response validates the core concern, reduces interactional intensity, and offers limited productive choices. A detailed policy explanation is hard to process during high arousal, while an immediate ultimatum may intensify the power struggle when no threat is present.

questions.prompt: What is the most appropriate intake response?

choices.A: Confirm the appointment but decline to discuss the content of future sessions
choices.B: Avoid confirming client status, preserve the information according to applicable practice procedures, and discuss collateral involvement with the client if the intake occurs
choices.C: Reply with the counselor's preliminary diagnosis so the roommate can provide additional observations

questions.scenarioContext: Before a client's first appointment, a roommate sends the counselor a detailed email describing the client's behavior and asks for confirmation that the client has scheduled counseling. The client has not authorized contact with the roommate.
questions.explanation: An unsolicited message does not authorize confirmation that the person is a client or permit disclosure to the sender. The counselor can handle the received information appropriately and later seek the client's perspective and permission regarding collateral involvement.

questions.prompt: How should the plan be revised?

choices.A: Continue the application objective unchanged until the original review date to preserve consistency
choices.B: Document the gain and collaboratively add an interview-preparation objective while maintaining useful application habits
choices.C: Close the employment goal because completing one objective demonstrates readiness to manage the remaining steps alone

questions.scenarioContext: A client in career counseling met an objective of submitting four job applications weekly ahead of schedule. The broader employment goal remains active, and the client now reports anxiety about interviewing.
questions.explanation: Meeting an objective early is information for progression, not a reason to retain a completed task or close the broader goal. The next objective should address the newly identified barrier while preserving behaviors that remain useful.

questions.prompt: What should the counselor do?

choices.A: Explore the client’s concern, explain how reminder information is handled, and let the client choose an acceptable reminder method.
choices.B: Continue texts because repeated neutral messages will gradually correct the client’s fear.
choices.C: Disable every electronic service without discussion to protect the client from further distress.

questions.scenarioContext: A refugee client becomes tense when automated appointment texts arrive and explains that electronic messages from institutions were used for surveillance in the client’s country of origin. The clinic offers telephone, email, text, or no automated reminders.
questions.explanation: The counselor links the present reaction to the client’s stated context, provides transparent information, and preserves choice among available methods. Continuing texts as involuntary exposure dismisses the surveillance history, while disabling everything without consultation also removes agency.

questions.prompt: What should the counselor do before signing the note?

choices.A: Remove the quotation marks and identify the content as the client's reported meaning
choices.B: Keep the quotation marks because the paraphrase accurately captures the client's intent
choices.C: Delete the statement because only exact quotations may appear in a progress note

questions.scenarioContext: While reviewing an unsigned note, a counselor realizes that a sentence placed inside quotation marks is a paraphrase of the client's statement rather than the client's exact words. The paraphrase is otherwise accurate.
questions.explanation: Quotation marks indicate exact language, which the counselor knows was not recorded. Identifying the sentence as a paraphrased client report preserves its accurate meaning without overstating precision. Useful reported content does not need to be deleted merely because it is not a direct quotation.

questions.prompt: What coordination approach best supports the client?

choices.A: Compare schedule alternatives with the client and authorized stakeholders while limiting communication to the participation issue
choices.B: Ask the client to leave the team because counseling should take precedence over extracurricular activities
choices.C: Explain the client's symptoms to the coach so the coach understands why schedule flexibility is necessary

questions.scenarioContext: A 16-year-old client wants to continue both a counseling skills group and the school basketball team, but their schedules overlap twice each month. The client and guardian authorize the counselor to coordinate scheduling with the school counselor and coach. The client does not want clinical details shared with the coach.
questions.explanation: The authorization supports focused logistical coordination that can preserve two activities the client values. Clinical details are not needed to compare schedules and identify workable accommodations. Requiring the client to abandon the team would bypass collaborative problem-solving.

questions.prompt: Which procedure most directly evaluates interrater reliability for an observational assessment?

choices.A: Administering the same instrument to the same clients again two weeks later
choices.B: Comparing scores assigned independently by two trained observers watching the same behavior
choices.C: Correlating the assessment with a different measure of the same construct

questions.explanation: Interrater reliability concerns agreement between evaluators observing the same target. Repeating a measure over time assesses test-retest reliability, while correlation with another construct measure addresses validity evidence.

questions.prompt: What is the main therapeutic function of a minimal encourager such as “Mm-hmm” or “Go on”?

choices.A: To communicate attention and invite the client to continue without directing the content.
choices.B: To indicate that the counselor agrees with the client’s interpretation.
choices.C: To move the client toward a topic the counselor considers more important.

questions.explanation: Minimal encouragers convey presence while leaving the client in control of what comes next. They do not necessarily signal agreement and should not covertly steer the client toward the counselor’s preferred topic.

questions.prompt: What should the counselor do?

choices.A: Promise the adolescent complete confidentiality so honest counseling can begin.
choices.B: Review the confidentiality agreement and its safety limits with both, explain how updates can be handled, and invite questions before proceeding.
choices.C: Ask the parent to leave immediately and discuss confidentiality only with the adolescent.

questions.scenarioContext: A 15-year-old begins counseling with a parent present. The parent says, “I expect to hear everything discussed here,” and the adolescent looks alarmed. The agency’s consent form allows private adolescent sessions and specifies the information that must be disclosed for safety.
questions.explanation: Clear orientation creates realistic expectations and supports trust for both adolescent and parent under the stated agency arrangement. Promising total secrecy is inaccurate, while removing the parent before explaining the framework can intensify confusion and conflict.

questions.prompt: Which diagnosis is best supported by these findings?

choices.A: Hoarding disorder
choices.B: Obsessive-compulsive personality disorder
choices.C: Specific phobia, situational type

questions.scenarioContext: A client has persistent difficulty discarding possessions regardless of value, intense distress when attempting to discard, and severe clutter that blocks the kitchen and one exit. The accumulation is not attributable to another medical condition or to another mental disorder.
questions.explanation: Persistent difficulty discarding, distress associated with discarding, and clutter that compromises living areas are defining features of hoarding disorder under the supplied exclusions. A personality style or situational fear does not account for the accumulation and blocked living space.

questions.prompt: What is the most appropriate response?

choices.A: Review progress and remaining needs, create a focused ending plan, and offer affordable continuation or reentry options
choices.B: Insist that the client complete the original course because early termination may weaken treatment gains
choices.C: End immediately without further planning because financial decisions fall outside the counseling relationship

questions.scenarioContext: A client with no acute safety concern says rising out-of-pocket costs require ending counseling earlier than planned. The client has made partial progress and wants to preserve gains but cannot continue at the current fee.
questions.explanation: The client has the right to end care, and the financial constraint can be addressed through a planned, clinically informed transition. Coercing completion or ending without review would fail to support maintenance of partial gains.

questions.prompt: What should the counselor do before providing counseling?

choices.A: Rely on the active license because licensure automatically supplies liability coverage
choices.B: Begin immediately and purchase coverage only if a client later files a complaint
choices.C: Verify appropriate coverage, authorization, and scope compliance for the volunteer setting

questions.scenarioContext: A licensed counselor wants to volunteer clinical services at a disaster shelter. The counselor's employer policy covers only work performed for the employer, and the shelter requires volunteers to confirm independent liability coverage and compliance with local scope rules.
questions.explanation: A license establishes professional authority only within applicable scope and does not itself provide insurance for every setting. The counselor should confirm both the shelter's requirements and independent coverage before beginning clinical work.

questions.prompt: How should the counselor assess decision-making capacity?

choices.A: Accept the family's conclusion because a psychotic disorder automatically eliminates capacity
choices.B: Evaluate the client's ability to understand information, appreciate its personal relevance, reason about options, and communicate a stable choice
choices.C: Determine capacity solely from whether the client agrees with the counselor's recommendation

questions.scenarioContext: A client with a chronic psychotic disorder is considering a voluntary outpatient program. The client can state a choice but gives inconsistent explanations of the program and how its risks and benefits apply personally. The family insists that the diagnosis itself proves incapacity.
questions.explanation: Capacity is decision specific and cannot be inferred solely from a psychiatric diagnosis or disagreement with a recommendation. The assessment should examine the functional abilities required for the actual decision.

questions.prompt: What is the most appropriate response?

choices.A: Keep the stricter consequence because the client's emotional reaction shows that the limit is effective
choices.B: Examine the personal meaning of lateness, consult as needed, repair the inconsistency, and apply policy based on clinical facts
choices.C: Avoid addressing attendance in the future because the counselor can no longer set an objective limit

questions.scenarioContext: A client repeatedly arrives late. The counselor, who grew up in a household where lateness was treated as disrespect, begins ending this client's sessions earlier than the agency attendance policy requires and feels satisfied when the client becomes upset.
questions.explanation: The counselor's history and satisfaction at the client's distress show that a personal reaction is shaping a harsher limit. Reflection, repair, and consistent application restore fairness while still allowing attendance to be addressed clinically.

questions.prompt: Which initial plan best balances the mandate and collaboration?

choices.A: Explain the required focus and confidentiality limits, then link alcohol-related review with the student's academic goal
choices.B: Use all six sessions only for alcohol education because required services cannot include client-selected goals
choices.C: Avoid discussing alcohol until the student independently identifies it as a problem

questions.scenarioContext: A university conduct program requires a student to attend six counseling sessions addressing consequences of alcohol use. The student does not agree that alcohol is the main problem but wants help improving grades after several missed classes. The program permits individualized goals in addition to the required focus.
questions.explanation: The counselor should be transparent about the mandated elements while using the flexibility allowed by the program to build client-relevant goals. Ignoring the required focus or excluding the student's academic concern would weaken informed collaboration.

questions.prompt: Which coordination response is most appropriate?

choices.A: With Andre's input, align counseling times with the dialysis schedule and establish a continuity plan for treatment-related disruptions
choices.B: Close Andre's counseling case because medical treatment makes regular attendance uncertain
choices.C: Ask the dialysis social worker to decide when Andre is emotionally ready for counseling

questions.scenarioContext: Andre receives hemodialysis three mornings per week and is often fatigued afterward. He has authorized coordination between his counselor and the dialysis social worker. Several afternoon counseling appointments have been canceled on treatment days, but Andre wants to continue counseling.
questions.explanation: The attendance pattern has a predictable treatment-related context that can be addressed through coordinated scheduling. A continuity plan respects Andre's wish to remain in counseling while preparing for disruptions. The dialysis social worker can collaborate but should not decide Andre's emotional readiness.

questions.prompt: What should the counselor do?

choices.A: Use the agency's immediate safety process, report objective observations, and help prevent impaired client contact
choices.B: Wait for group members to complain so the counselor has evidence of actual harm
choices.C: Keep the concern private because reporting a colleague always violates professional loyalty

questions.scenarioContext: A counselor observes a colleague smelling strongly of alcohol, speaking unclearly, and preparing to conduct a group session. Agency policy requires immediate supervisor notification and removal from client contact when impairment may create a safety risk.
questions.explanation: The observed signs and imminent group session create the safety risk described by agency policy. Waiting for actual harm would leave clients exposed, while a factual report avoids speculation about the colleague's diagnosis.

questions.prompt: Which intervention best matches the client’s stated goal?

choices.A: Require an abstinence commitment because moderation plans communicate approval of substance use.
choices.B: Focus on why the client is unwilling to choose the goal most likely to eliminate risk.
choices.C: Develop a concrete harm-reduction plan addressing drink limits, nonalcoholic alternatives, and transportation before the event.

questions.scenarioContext: A client has decided to reduce alcohol use at social events rather than pursue abstinence. The client identifies free drinks and lack of transportation as situations that often lead to drinking more than intended.
questions.explanation: The client has chosen a reduction goal and identified predictable risk conditions, so a specific plan can lower harm and support self-monitoring. Imposing abstinence would override the stated goal and may reduce engagement.

questions.prompt: How should the counselor manage the collaboration?

choices.A: Reconfirm Tariq's desired involvement and establish a structured update schedule and relevant content with the mentor
choices.B: Accept all daily messages because more collateral information always improves counseling decisions
choices.C: End the mentor's involvement without consulting Tariq because the messages are too frequent

questions.scenarioContext: Tariq has authorized a volunteer recovery mentor to participate in support planning. The mentor begins sending the counselor long daily messages about Tariq's routine, although Tariq originally requested only a weekly update about attendance at community activities.
questions.explanation: Tariq should continue to define how the mentor participates in his support plan. A clear schedule and content boundary can preserve useful collaboration without allowing excessive collateral material to drive counseling. Ending the relationship unilaterally would also disregard Tariq's choice.

questions.prompt: What should the counselor do?

choices.A: Proceed with headphones because they prevent other people from hearing both sides
choices.B: Proceed without video so nearby travelers cannot identify the client
choices.C: Move to a compliant private setup or reschedule the appointment

questions.scenarioContext: A counselor has a telehealth appointment during an airport layover. The only available seating is public, and the network is open Wi-Fi. Practice policy requires a private setting and an approved secure connection for telehealth.
questions.explanation: Both the public setting and open network fail the practice's stated safeguards. Headphones or audio-only communication cannot protect what the counselor says, the screen, or the network transmission.

questions.prompt: What should the records lead recommend?

choices.A: Decommission the old system because most clinical notes transferred successfully
choices.B: Halt decommissioning, reconcile the discrepancies, and verify record completeness and integrity first
choices.C: Ask counselors to recreate missing information from memory after the old system is erased

questions.scenarioContext: During migration to a new electronic health record, sample testing shows missing consent forms and altered service dates. Management wants to shut down the old system that evening to avoid another licensing fee.
questions.explanation: Missing forms and changed dates show that the migration has not preserved reliable records. Deleting the source system before reconciliation could make errors permanent and impair care, access, and compliance.

questions.prompt: What is the best intake decision?

choices.A: Enroll the person now because attendance expectations should be discussed only after group begins
choices.B: Explain the group's structure and attendance expectations and explore the later group or another suitable service
choices.C: Deny all agency services because anticipated absences show resistance to counseling

questions.scenarioContext: A prospective member wants to join a closed 12-session coping-skills group but expects to miss the first four meetings because of travel. The group builds each week's exercises on material from earlier sessions, and an identical group will begin the following month.
questions.explanation: The cumulative closed-group format makes missing the first third of meetings clinically and practically relevant to suitability. Transparent discussion and an available later group address the mismatch without treating travel as resistance or denying all services.
